thread.title: Stock market news: Jan. 29, 2019

author: Emily McCormick
title: Stock market news: Jan. 29, 2019
text:
Stocks were mixed as investors awaited a slew of stimuli including U.S.-China trade talks, the Federal Open Market Committee’s latest policy decision and a host of quarterly reports from some of the biggest names in the S&P 500.
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped 0.15%, or 3.86 points, as of market close. The Dow ( ^DJI ) rose 0.21%, or 51.81 points, while the Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) declined 0.81%, or 57.39 points.
Earnings season charges forward, with 36 companies comprising 10% of the S&P 500’s market capitalization set to report on Tuesday. Among the companies reporting include Apple ( AAPL ), Pfizer ( PFE ), Amgen ( AMGN ), 3M ( MMM ) and Yahoo’s parent-company Verizon ( VZ ).
As of Tuesday morning, 27.7% of the S&P 500’s market cap had reported fourth-quarter results, with earnings beating by 2%, and 65% of companies exceeding their bottom-line estimates, Credit Suisse Chief Equity Strategist Jonathan Golub wrote in a note. This compares to 4.9% and 70% over the past three years.
A host of global developments are weighing on investors. Stock futures have largely recovered from overnight declines, spurred after U.S. authorities Monday evening unveiled a set of criminal charges against China’s telecom giant Huawei Technologies. Federal prosecutors accused Huawei of committing bank fraud in breaching U.S. sanctions on Iran and stealing trade secrets from T-Mobile. The U.S. Department of Justice also filed criminal charges against Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s CFO who in early December was arrested in Canada at the request of the U.S.
The criminal charges add fuel to the Trump administration’s efforts to combat alleged intellectual property theft in China, which has been a central concern as the administration attempts to hammer out a trade deal with the country. However, the indictments have drawn the ire of China, which denied the charges and accused the U.S. of trying to “kill” Chinese businesses, threatening to complicate negotiations ahead of a two-day meeting between Chinese Vice Premier Liu He and U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer in Washington, D.C.
Tuesday also marks the first of two days of meetings for the Federal Open Market Committee. The FOMC on Wednesday will release a statement announcing its latest decision of whether or not to raise the target range of its short-term interest rates from the current band of 2.25% to 2.5%. Consensus economists anticipate the central bank will pause on hiking rates following this month’s meeting amid slow global growth, trade tensions and fourth-quarter market volatility.
STOCKS: 3M beats expectations, PG&E files for bankruptcy protection Manufacturing giant 3M ( MMM ) beat Wall Street’s expectations for fourth- quarter results. The company posted quarterly revenue of $7.95 billion, ahead of Bloomberg-compiled estimates of $7.86 billion, and delivered adjusted quarterly earnings of $2.31 per share, or about three cents better-than-expected. The maker of Post-It notes said it saw organic sales growth of 3%, including expansion across all business groups and geographic areas, excluding currency impacts. The broad geographic growth was well-received by investors amid warning signs flashed by Caterpillar ( CAT ), another global bellwether, about soft demand in China. However, 3M cut its earnings guidance for full-year 2019 to be in the range of $10.45 to $10.90 per share, from $10.60 to $11.05 per share previously. 3M said the revision was made in part to include impacts of the pending acquisition of tech business MModal, which had previously not been included in guidance.
Specialist Meric Greenbaum, center, works with traders at his post on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Monday, Jan. 28, 2019. (AP Photo/Richard Drew) More Harley-Davidson ( HOG ), a motorcycle manufacturer long caught in the crosshairs of the Trump administration’s trade war, missed Wall Street’s estimates on the top and bottom lines for the fourth quarter. Adjusted earnings per share were 17 cents on revenue of $955.63 million, falling short of consensus estimates of 29 cents on sales of $1.05 billion. Including restructuring and tariff costs, EPS was zero for the fourth-quarter. Aside from tariff concerns, Harley-Davidson also faced dropping retail demand in Europe and Asia, which sent global sales down 6.7% in the quarter.
